title: Watching Too Much TV May Shrink Your Brain
paragraphs: Spending your evenings in front of the TV may seem like a harmless way to relax. However, a new long-term study from the United States suggests that watching a lot of television in middle age may be linked to a smaller brain later in life.

The study was published in the journal Alzheimer's & Dementia in 2026, and it was led by researchers including Natan Feter and David Raichlen. It used data from the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities study, a long-running project that tracks heart and brain health in several US communities.

Between 1987 and 1989, the participants, who were about 53 years old on average, answered questions about how often they watched TV in their free time and how often they sat down at work. More than 20 years later, when they were about 76, 1,712 of them had brain scans.

The researchers found that people who said they watched TV very often had less gray matter in two parts of the brain, the frontal and occipital lobes. They also had less volume in a group of brain areas that are affected early by Alzheimer's disease. In addition, they had more signs of damage to the brain's white matter. These links remained even after the researchers took physical activity into account.

Interestingly, sitting at work had the opposite effect. People who always sat at work actually had larger brain volumes and less white matter damage than people who rarely sat at work. The researchers suggest that this may be because desk work is often mentally demanding, while watching TV is passive. However, this idea has not been proven.
The links were mainly found in men. Women did not show the same widespread changes, and the reasons for this difference are not known.

The study also had several limitations. The participants reported their own TV habits, and the questionnaire asked how often they watched TV rather than how many hours. In addition, there were no brain scans at the start of the study. As a result, the study shows a link between watching TV and brain size, but it cannot prove that TV causes the brain to shrink.
